title: Waves and Sound: Oscillations That Carry Energy

questions.question: A travelling wave transports:
questions.rationale: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy without carrying matter — the cork bobs in place as ripples pass.

questions.question: Sound in air is best classified as a:
questions.rationale: Sound is longitudinal (compressions and rarefactions along the travel direction) and mechanical — it needs a medium.

questions.question: Using v = fλ, the wavelength of a 500 Hz note in air (343 m/s) is about:
questions.rationale: λ = 343 ÷ 500 ≈ 0.69 m, the spacing between successive compressions, as the lesson's example computes.

questions.question: In which order does the speed of sound increase?
options: The speed is the same in all three
questions.rationale: The lesson's chart shows about 343 m/s in air, 1500 m/s in water, and 5000 m/s in steel.

questions.question: The loudness of a sound depends mainly on its:
questions.rationale: Loudness tracks amplitude; pitch tracks frequency and quality (timbre) tracks waveform.

questions.question: The audible range of the healthy human ear is roughly:
questions.rationale: Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; below is infrasound and above is ultrasound.

questions.question: The minimum distance of a reflecting surface for a clear echo at 20 °C is about:
questions.rationale: With a 0.1 s persistence of hearing, d = 343 × 0.1 ÷ 2 ≈ 17.2 m.

questions.question: A SONAR pulse returns after 2 s. With sound at 1500 m/s in sea water, the depth is:
questions.rationale: d = vt ÷ 2 = 1500 × 2 ÷ 2 = 1,500 m — the lesson's worked SONAR example.

questions.question: As an ambulance with a blaring siren approaches you, the pitch you hear:
questions.rationale: The Doppler effect raises the apparent frequency of an approaching source and lowers it as the source recedes.

questions.question: The Mach number of a source is defined as:
options: Speed of light ÷ speed of sound
questions.rationale: Mach number is the ratio of source speed to the speed of sound; exceeding Mach 1 piles the wavefronts into a cone, creating a sonic boom.
